items.extracted_text_for_analysis: The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware. Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance. You can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201). - In the Overview tab, compare quantizations for one hardware, model, and build. The two charts show PP512 (512 input tokens, no generation) and TG128 (128 generated tokens), both starting at context depth zero. - In the Build history tab, track PP512 and TG128 across all recorded builds for the selected hardware, model, and quantization. - In the Context scaling tab, see how token-generation throughput changes as the existing context grows, for the selected build, hardware, model, and quantization. The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second: Both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows. We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration. The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16. The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model. Standard results use / / / .jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder -tg.jsonl filename. Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run. Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard, inspect the data, and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

items.extracted_title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference
items.extracted_excerpt: A Blog post by NVIDIA on Hugging Face
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference. We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process. We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training: - Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples: rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values. - Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples: rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships. - OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples: synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading. Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language. Figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents. We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content. A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output. Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods. The matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer—and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35. Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts. A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs. NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory. The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens, or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token. Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details. In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively. Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it: - Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts. - Double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output. - Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests. In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements. We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT, and NeMo RL GRPO, using vLLM to generate candidate answers. The worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram: a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth. Figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label. RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the

items.title_en: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems

items.extracted_title: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems
items.extracted_excerpt: We’re on a journey to advance and democratize artificial intelligence through open source and open science.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models. That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50. Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents? In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from. First, we'll start off with some context on swarms. We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem. But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so. A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment, coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same. Start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries. Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided. This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute? We understand that question through this simple expectation. We'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily. Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms. A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture. This creates three practical problems. First, teammates keep changing while each agent learns. Second, credit assignment: when the team succeeds, which actions deserve the credit? A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training. A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward. Agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are: - A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog. - A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL. We'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows. Each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is: #### [5, 5, 26, 78] The team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list. One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates. This means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? items.extracted_excerpt: Sakana Marlinアップデート：調査の深さと速さを引き上げる新モード「Twilight 2.0」「Midnight 2.0」と、スライド出力の刷新
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Sakana AIは本日、「Sakana Marlin」をアップデートし、調査の深さ・速さ・広さを引き上げる2つの新モード「Twilight 2.0」「Midnight 2.0」を追加しました。あわせて、Microsoft PowerPoint形式でのスライド出力機能も大幅に刷新しています。 - Twilight 2.0：より短時間で、多角的な検討を - Midnight 2.0：最も広い視野で、新たな発見を なお、従来のSakana Marlinは、軽量な「Sunlight」モードとして引き続きご利用いただけます。 海は、深さによってその姿を変えます。太陽の光が届く浅い層は「Sunlight zone」、わずかな光だけが届く層は「Twilight zone」、そして光がまったく届かない深い層は「Midnight zone」と呼ばれます。リサーチも同様に、表層で手に入る情報もあれば、深く潜ることで初めて見えてくる構造があります。3つのモード名は、この海の層に由来しています。 3つのモード名の由来となった、海の層 Sakana Marlinのコンセプト 今年6月に公開した「Sakana Marlin」のコンセプトは、「リサーチはAIへ。人間は意思決定に集中する。」です。調査テーマを指示するだけで、仮説立案から情報収集、検証、レポート作成までをAIが自律的に行う戦略リサーチエージェントとして、不確実な環境で重要な決断に向き合う方々を支えてきました。 提供開始以来、戦略立案、市場・競合分析、規制動向の調査など、幅広い業務でご活用いただいています。9月には、レポートと出典を行き来しながらAIと対話できる「Interactive Reading」やPowerPointスライド出力を追加し、調査結果を深く理解し、確信を持って次のアクションにつなげる体験を強化してきました。 深さとスピード、その両方に応えるために ご利用が広がるなかで、調査の深さ・速さ・広さのそれぞれについて、さらに高い水準を求める声を多くいただくようになりました。 - 会議の前に、まずは全体像をすばやく把握したい - すでに知見のある領域で、さらに踏み込んだ分析や多角的な観点がほしい 初期的な全体把握から専門領域の深掘りまで、重視すべき軸は調査の目的やフェーズによって異なります。 同時に、AI技術も急速に進化しています。推論時により多くの計算量を投じてアウトプットの質を引き上げる「推論時スケーリング」は、この数ヶ月でAI開発の主流になりつつあり、Sakana Marlinも当初からこの考え方を土台にしてきました（技術的な詳細はベータリリース時のブログをご覧ください）。 ただし、当時もお伝えしたとおり、計算量に比例して成果が上がるわけではありません。正解が一つに定まらない現実のリサーチでは、「何をもって良い調査とするか」という品質評価そのものが極めて難しいからです。評価の軸が定まらないまま推論を重ねても、アウトプットの質は安定しません。「より長く考えさせること」と「より良く考えさせること」は、決して同じではないのです。 1. 新モード「Twilight 2.0」「Midnight 2.0」：より速く、より深く、より広く 今回のアップデートでは、私たちが培ってきた推論時スケーリングの知見と、複雑で高度な知的生産におけるAIアウトプットの評価手法を組み合わせました。従来以上に推論を重ねることで、その分野の専門家にも新たな示唆をもたらす深さと広さに到達します。 新しいモードでは、調査の過程で得た情報をもとにAIが自ら問いを立て直し、仮説を更新しながら深掘りを続けます。一つの結論に安易に飛びつくのではなく、「本当にそう言えるのか」「別の可能性はないのか」と検証を繰り返しながら、「良い調査とは何か」という姿勢そのものを、リサーチのプロセスに組み込みました。 従来のSunlightを加えた3つのモードから、用途に応じて速さと深さを使い分けられます。 - Twilight 2.0：対象テーマの全体像と構造を、素早く広く捉えます。次の会議までに急いで論点を押さえたいときや、新規プロジェクトに向けて未知の領域をスピーディに俯瞰したい場面に適しています。 - Midnight 2.0：論点の網羅性と探索の深さ、そして高い検証力を備えています。すでに知見のある分野から新たなインサイトを引き出したいときや、徹底的な裏付けと専門的な深掘りが求められるシーンに最適です。 - Sunlight：従来のSakana Marlinです。コストを抑えて調査を完了させたい一般的な用途に向けて、引き続き提供します。 1回の調査で消費するクレジットは、Sunlightが100、Twilight 2.0とMidnight 2.0が300です。 Twilight 2.0はSunlightより1時間以上短い時間で約3倍の出典にあたり、Midnight 2.0は約7倍の出典にあたり、約5倍のボリュームのレポートを生成します。 3つのモードの処理時間、本文の長さ、引用した出典の数 新しいモードは、調査を依頼する際に選択するだけでご利用いただけます。 調査を依頼するときに、モードを選択する 2. スライド出力の刷新：長いレポートの要点を、スライドだけで伝える 2つ目のアップデートは、PowerPointスライド出力の刷新です。Sunlight、Twilight 2.0、Midnight 2.0のすべてのモードでご利用いただけます。 Twilight 2.0とMidnight 2.0によって調査が深まった分、レポートのボリュームも増えました。全文を読む時間が取れないときや会議で共有するとき、要点を凝縮したスライドの重要性はこれまで以上に高まっています。 そこで、スライドだけを見ても調査の全体像をつかめるよう、生成プロセスを根本から強化しました。AIエージェントがスライドを作成するためのハーネスを新たに開発し、プロフェッショナル水準の資料作成に必要な知見を組み込んでいます。エージェントはレポート全体を読み込んでストーリーを設計し、スライドを組み立てたうえで、出力結果を自ら確認してブラッシュアップを行います。 スライドは表紙・目次・エグゼクティブサマリーから始まり、レポート全体を一つのストーリーとして構成します。一枚ごとに伝えたいメッセージをリード文で明確に言い切り、論点の構造や因果関係は図解に、定量データはグラフに整理して出典URLを添えます。社内やクライアント指定のスライドテンプレートにも引き続き対応しており、同じ内容を所定のフォーマットで出力可能です。 新しい出力スライドの例 どれほど調査が深くても、伝わらなければ意思決定にはつながりません。「深く調べること」と「端的に伝えること」。新しいスライドは、その両方を1回の調査で届けるためのアップデートです。 サンプルレポートをご覧ください 新しいモードでアウトプットがどう変わったかは、実際のレポートをご覧いただくのが一番です。プロダクトページでは、Sakana Marlinが作成したサンプルレポートとスライドを公開しています。ぜひダウンロードしてご覧ください。 サンプルレポートを見る： https://sakana.ai/marlin/#usecase Sakana AIのプロダクトは、これからも人とAIが調和し、高度な意思決定を実現できる世界を目指していきます。 Sakana Marlinは、従量課金プランからTeam・Enterpriseプランまでご用意しています。料金や各モードの消費クレジット、最新情報については、プロダクトページをご覧ください。 Sakana Marlinを試す： https://sakana.ai/marlin/ Sakana Marlinの最新情報： https://sakana.ai/marlin/news/ ※ Microsoft、PowerPointは、マイクロソフト グループの企業の商標です。 Sakana AI Sakana AIは、AIの未来を私たちと一緒に切り拓いてくださる方を募集しています。当社の募集要項をご覧ください。 English Announcement Sakana Marlin Update: Twilight 2.0 and Midnight 2.0, Two New Modes for Faster and Deeper Research, plus Redesigned Slides Today Sakana AI is updating Sakana Marlin with two new research modes, Twilight 2.0 and Midnight 2.0, that raise the depth, speed and breadth of its research. We have also substantially improved the quality of the slides it exports in Microsoft PowerPoint format. - Twilight 2.0: More angles, in less time - Midnight 2.0: The widest view, for new discoveries The Sakana Marlin you have been using remains available as Sunlight, a lighter mode. The ocean changes with depth. The shallow layer that sunlight reaches is called the sunlight zone, the layer where only faint light arrives is the twilight zone, and the deep layer that no light reaches at all is the midnight zone. Research is similar: some information can be found near the surface, and some structures only come into view when you dive deep. The three modes take their names from these layers of the sea. The layers of the sea that give the three modes their names The Idea Behind Sakana Marlin When we launched Sakana Marlin in June, we described it in a single line: leave the research to AI, so people can focus on the decision making. Sakana Marlin is a strategic research agent. Give it a topic, and it works autonomously from framing hypotheses through gathering and testing evidence to writing up the findings as a report, in support of people facing big decisions in uncertain times. Since launch, it has been used for strategy work, market and competitor analysis, regulatory research and much else. In September we added Interactive Reading, which lets you move between a report and its sources while talking with the AI, and PowerPoint slide export. With them we have been strengthening the experience of understanding the findings deeply, confirming them and turning them into action. Answering the Call for Both Depth and Speed As more people came to rely on Sakana Marlin, we heard more and more requests for a higher standard of depth, speed and breadth: - “Before a meeting, I want to grasp the big picture quickly.” - “In a field I know well, I want analysis that goes further, and more angles on the question.” From a first overview to a deep dive in a specialist field, which of these matters most depends on the purpose and the stage of the research. AI technology has been moving quickly too. Over the past few months, inference-time scaling, in which a system spends more compute at inference time to raise the quality of its output, has been moving into the mainstream of AI development. Sakana Marlin has been built on this idea from the start. Technical details are available in our beta-release blog post. But as we wrote then, results do not improve in proportion to the compute put in. In real-world research, where no single right answer exists, it is hard to say what makes research good in the first place: evaluating quality is itself the difficult part. Without a settled way to judge the output, piling on more inference does not produce stable quality. Thinking longer is not the same as thinking better. 1. New Modes, Twilight 2.0 and Midnight 2.0: Faster, Deeper and Broader Research For this update we brought together two bodies of know-how: what we have learned about inference-time scaling, and what we have learned about evaluating the output of AI on complex, demanding intellectual work in the real world. The result is two new modes that spend even more inference than before and reach a depth and breadth that offer new insight

items.extracted_title: Distilling Kimi-K3.1-Pro into Qwen3.8-27B: Teaching a model a new language
items.extracted_excerpt: Qwen3.8-27B answered in Thai when asked for Lao. We distilled Kimi-K3.1-Pro's Lao translation into it with Together Post-Training: 93% of the teacher's score, with Thai intact. Code and costs included.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: - The gap: Qwen3.8-27B answers in Thai when asked for Lao and scores 5.5 chrF++, while Kimi-K3.1-Pro scores 47.5 on the same test. - The fix: We trained a LoRA adapter on about 3,800 of Kimi-K3.1-Pro's translations using Together Post-Training. - The result: The student writes Lao on every test sentence and scores 44.3, which is 93% of the teacher's score, and it keeps its Thai. - The cost: All the experiments together cost \$260, and the code is in the post-training cookbook. While running some experiments we found out that Qwen3.8-27B, one of the most popular small language models (SLMs), can't write Lao, a Southwestern Tai language and the official language of Laos. If you ask it to translate an English sentence into Lao, it answers in Thai, Lao's closest relative, which uses an entirely different script. On the FLORES-200 Lao test set, the model scores 5.5 chrF++, a 0 to 100 score for how closely a translation matches a human reference, and only 11% of its outputs are in Lao script. Kimi-K3.1-Pro scores 47.5 on the same test. Admittedly, this is a niche use case, but the pattern is quite common: a small language model displays jagged intelligence, falling flat on a narrow task you care about while a larger, more expensive model handles it with ease. To fix this, we used Kimi-K3.1-Pro as a teacher and distilled its Lao translation ability into Qwen3.8-27B using Together Post-Training. After training on about 3,800 of Kimi-K3.1-Pro's translations, the 27B student answers in Lao on every test sentence and scores 44.3, which is 93% of the teacher's score. It also kept its Thai translation ability, which interestingly turned out to be the hardest part. Our first attempt fixed Lao within 25 training steps but also lost Thai translating capabilities along with it. This post walks through how we found the gap and what ended up working. The code, settings and costs are in the second half. All the experiments together cost \$260. Finding the gap The metric we use is chrF++, which scores character and word overlap with a human reference translation, from 0 to 100. The important thing to know about Qwen's low Lao score is that, to chrF++, a Thai answer shares almost nothing with a Lao reference. When asked to translate into Lao, the student's output contained Thai script in 45 of 50 sentences and Lao in only 6: English: "We now have 4-month-old mice that are non-diabetic that used to be diabetic," he added. Qwen3.8-27B (base): “ปัจจุบันเรามีหนูอายุ 4 เดือนที่ไม่เป็นโรคเบาหวาน ซึ่งเคยเป็นโรคเบาหวานมาก่อน” เขากล่าวเสริม Kimi-K3.1-Pro: "ພວກເຮົາຕອນນີ້ມີໜູອາຍຸ 4 ເດືອນ ທີ່ບໍ່ເປັນໂຣກເບົາຫວານ ເຊິ່ງເຄີຍເປັນໂຣກເບົາຫວານມາກ່ອນ," ລາວກ່າວຕື່ມ. The base model's Thai is a reasonable translation, just in the wrong language. We'll come back to this in the results. One note on the numbers: on these 50 sentences Lao scores 7.2 for Qwen3.8-27B and 49.0 for Kimi-K3.1-Pro, and on the full 1,012-sentence test set it's 5.5 and 47.5. The test sets are listed under "How we built it." The plan: off-policy distillation Distillation trains a small model (the student) to behave like a large one (the teacher) on a given domain. There are two ways to do it. On-policy distillation (OPD), described in Thinking Machines' post on the topic, has the student generate text and the teacher grade every token. It needs the teacher's log-probabilities on the student's tokens, which in practice means the two models have to share a tokenizer. Here since we are distilling Kimi into Qwen and they don’t share a tokenizer we went another direction. Off-policy distillation has the teacher generate the text and trains the student to imitate it with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In its simplest form it only needs the teacher's text. We used off-policy distillation. It keeps the teacher side fairly cheap: every teacher call is an ordinary serverless chat request, and Kimi-K3.1-Pro, which is quite a large model, never needs a training resource of its own. The steps: - Collect English source sentences. - Have Kimi-K3.1-Pro translate them, with thinking turned off. - Drop any translation that isn't mostly in the target script. - Fine-tune a LoRA adapter on Qwen3.8-27B with the translations as targets, evaluating on held-out test sentences as it trains. - Save the adapter to the model registry. We trained the student on Together Post-Training. One model resource both trains the LoRA adapter and samples from it, so we could score the model as it trained. We scored every evaluation on four metrics: - chrF++ against human references on FLORES-200 devtest: all 1,012 sentences at the start and end of each run, and 300 every 25 steps (every 50 or 100 in the two longest runs). - Lao-script rate: the share of outputs whose letters are mostly Lao. This catches the Thai problem directly. - Thai retention: chrF++ on 300 English-to-Thai test sentences, to check the model hasn't lost a language it already had. - Round-trip adequacy: Kimi-K3.1-Pro translates each system's Lao back into English, and we score that against the original English. This checks meaning independently of reference style. Thai retention while also gaining Lao translation capability ended up being the trickiest part. The Thai surprise One run was a control: it trained on human Lao references, 945 of them from FLORES dev, with no teacher involved. Lao jumped from 6.7 to 43.3 within 25 steps. Then we looked at Thai. It had dropped from 46.7 to 11.7, and by the end of the run it was 5.3, with 0% of Thai outputs in Thai script. The model had learned to "write Lao when asked to translate", not "write the language you were asked for". The problem had swapped direction. If we'd evaluated Lao alone, this run would have looked like the winner. It has the highest Lao score of any student in this post. Fixing Thai The Lao-only distillation run trains on Kimi-K3.1-Pro's translations of the same sentences in place of the human ones. That slowed the damage a lot but didn't stop it. Thai held for two epochs, then slipped to 44.3 in the third, with 17 of 300 Thai answers written in Lao. Adding about 1,000 Kimi-K3.1-Pro Thai translations to the training data fixed it. Thai finished at 47.4 and 47.8 in the two mixed runs, above the base model, and never dropped below 47.3 at any evaluation. This is a great point to make about continual learning: when you teach a model something new, mix in data that protects what it already does well, so you don't get regressions in things you care about. Here that was Thai, the language most easily confused with Lao. Closing the rest of the Lao gap Thai was safe, but Lao was still short. With about 950 Lao examples each, the student trained on human references scored 44.7 and the two distilled students scored 41.8 and 41.9. Part of that is expected. Human references do better on a human-reference metric: FLORES dev and devtest were translated through the same human process, so training on dev teaches devtest's reference style. evidence_zh.text: Distilling Kimi-K3.1-Pro into Qwen3.8-27B: Teaching a model a new language

evidence_zh.label: 公开摘要
evidence_zh.text: Qwen3.8-27B answered in Thai when asked for Lao. We distilled Kimi-K3.1-Pro's Lao translation into it with Together Post-Training: 93% of the teacher's score, with Thai intact. Code and costs included.
